chapter: Big bands, Depression work and the WPA band
title: Depression pay and plentiful jobs
summary: More musicians worked during the Depression than ever, for a dollar to three dollars a night. When beer returned in 1933 small bands multiplied.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: No, that was during the Depression. During the Depression. Right. And matter of fact, they had more musicians working during the Depression than they ever did have. Because I mean, the odd of this, it was so rough, he was going playing for a dollar a night. Yeah. A dollar a night.
We had the biggest job on the Crescent City, a dollar and a half a night. That's right. That's right. Biggest job in town.
And go all the way on the Christmas Eve night playing back in Los Angeles for three dollars. And they was fighting for the job. Yeah.
He could eat on a dollar a day.
A dollar a day could last you a week. Plus they was giving you cars to get food with and they said...
I was going to get out of the mobile on Mondays, I think we'd make it six or eight dollars, something like that. Rich. Random money. Don't be telling me.
Yeah. That's right. And I mean, see, in 33 when Bill was brought back, all the little Bill Paul was throwing three and four pieces every Friday and Saturday. Oh yeah, everything would jump up.
It was hard to get them using me because everybody had a job on the weekend, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, three dollars extra a week, man. That was big money.
You see, before they brought all the men around the street, I said, leave them five out of the night and go to my mom, leave my mom, go to Kingfish, leave Kingfish and go to the Rose Bowl.
